title: Acids, bases, conjugate pairs and amphiprotic species
html:
Guiding question

Guiding question: What happens when protons are transferred?

Acid–base chemistry is the chemistry of the proton. A hydrogen ion, H⁺, is just a bare proton (a hydrogen atom that has lost its only electron), so every acid–base reaction in this topic is a proton transfer from one species (the acid) to another (the base). Everything that follows – pH, Kw, strong and weak acids, titration curves, buffers – is a way of describing how far and how easily that transfer happens.

Start with what you already know from earlier courses. Before we look at theory, try the "do now" questions the lesson opens with.

Do now: what is an acid, a base and an alkali? Is water any of these?
  • Acid: a substance with pH below 7 in water that produces H⁺(aq) ions; in Brønsted–Lowry terms, a proton donor.
  • Base: a substance that reacts with (neutralizes) the H⁺ ions of an acid; a proton acceptor.
  • Alkali: a base that dissolves in water, producing OH⁻(aq) ions.
  • Water can be both: it can donate a proton (to NH₃) or accept one (from HCl). Species like this are amphiprotic – the end of this lesson.

Indicators you have met before

Simple indicators tell us whether a solution is acidic, neutral or alkaline:

IndicatorIn acidIn neutralIn alkali
blue litmusturns redstays bluestays blue
red litmusstays redstays redturns blue
methyl orangeredyellow (orange at the change, pH ≈ 3–4)yellow
phenolphthaleincolourlesscolourlesspink (above pH ≈ 8.3)

Acids and bases have opposite properties and neutralize each other when mixed. Quantitative work (R3.1.8 and the AHL sections) explains why each indicator changes colour where it does.

R3.1.1 Brønsted–Lowry acids and bases

DefinitionA Brønsted–Lowry acid is a proton (H⁺) donor. A Brønsted–Lowry base is a proton (H⁺) acceptor.

Because H⁺ ions are protons, an acid–base reaction is a proton transfer from the acid to the base. To accept a proton, a base must have a lone pair of electrons that can form a coordination bond to H⁺. In water the donated proton bonds to a water molecule, forming the hydronium (oxonium, hydroxonium) ion, H₃O⁺. H⁺(aq) and H₃O⁺(aq) are used interchangeably in equations.

HA(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₃O⁺(aq) + A⁻(aq)     (acid in water)
B(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ BH⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq)     (base in water)

The older Arrhenius idea (acids produce H⁺ in water, bases produce OH⁻) is narrower. Brønsted–Lowry theory does not need water at all:

  • HCl is an acid in both theories: HCl(aq) → H⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq).
  • NH₃ reacting with HCl gas, NH₃(g) + HCl(g) → NH₄Cl(s), is a Brønsted–Lowry acid–base reaction (HCl donates H⁺ to NH₃) even though no water or OH⁻ is involved, so ammonia is a Brønsted–Lowry base but not an Arrhenius base. You see this as the white "smoke" of solid ammonium chloride where the two gases meet.
TheoryAcidBaseLimitation
Arrheniusproduces H⁺ in waterproduces OH⁻ in wateronly aqueous solutions; NH₃(g) + HCl(g) not covered
Brønsted–Lowryproton donorproton acceptorneeds a transferable H⁺
Lewis (R3.4)electron-pair acceptorelectron-pair donorbroadest; includes reactions with no H⁺ at all

What is happening in these two reactions?

  • Ethanoic acid + water: CH₃COOH donates H⁺ to H₂O, so CH₃COOH is the acid and water is the base. Water uses a lone pair on its O atom to bond to the H⁺, so it is also acting as a Lewis base.
  • Ammonia + water: H₂O donates H⁺ to NH₃, so water is the acid and ammonia the base. Ammonia uses the lone pair on N, so it is also a Lewis base (see R3.4).
CH₃COOH(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ CH₃COO⁻(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq)      NH₃(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ NH₄⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq)

Alkali = a base that dissolves in water to give OH⁻ ions (e.g. NaOH, KOH, Ca(OH)₂, aqueous NH₃). Metal oxides and carbonates that are insoluble are bases but not alkalis. So all alkalis are bases, but not all bases are alkalis.

In the reaction NH₃(g) + HCl(g) → NH₄Cl(s), which statement is correct?

  1. NH₃ is an Arrhenius base and a Brønsted–Lowry base
  2. NH₃ is a Brønsted–Lowry base but not an Arrhenius base
  3. HCl is acting as a base
  4. No proton transfer occurs because there is no water

HCl donates H⁺ to the lone pair on N, so NH₃ accepts a proton: a Brønsted–Lowry base. No water is present and no OH⁻ is produced, so the Arrhenius definition does not apply.

R3.1.2 Conjugate acid–base pairs

DefinitionA conjugate acid–base pair is two species that differ by a single proton (H⁺). The acid loses H⁺ to become its conjugate base; the base gains H⁺ to become its conjugate acid.

Every Brønsted–Lowry reaction has two conjugate pairs, one on each side of the arrow, because the reverse reaction is also a proton transfer:

Worked exampleHCN(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₃O⁺(aq) + CN⁻(aq)
  1. Forward reaction: HCN donates H⁺ → HCN is an acid; H₂O accepts H⁺ → H₂O is a base.
  2. Reverse reaction: H₃O⁺ donates H⁺ → acid; CN⁻ accepts H⁺ → base.
  3. Pairs: HCN / CN⁻ and H₃O⁺ / H₂O (always write acid first).
  • A strong acid is a good proton donor and has a very weak conjugate base (Cl⁻ has almost no tendency to take H⁺ back).
  • A strong base is a good proton acceptor and has a very weak conjugate acid.
  • The weaker the acid, the stronger its conjugate base (CH₃COO⁻ is a noticeably basic ion).
Common mistakeA conjugate pair differs by H⁺ (a proton), not by H (a hydrogen atom) and not by "a positive charge". The conjugate base of OH⁻ is O²⁻; the conjugate acid of OH⁻ is H₂O.

Acid–base pair task. Write the conjugate partner of each species, then check.

SpeciesConjugate baseConjugate acid
H₂OOH⁻H₃O⁺
NH₃NH₂⁻NH₄⁺
HSO₄⁻SO₄²⁻H₂SO₄
HCO₃⁻CO₃²⁻H₂CO₃
H₂PO₄⁻HPO₄²⁻H₃PO₄

What is the conjugate base of H₂PO₄⁻?

  1. H₃PO₄
  2. HPO₄²⁻
  3. PO₄³⁻
  4. H₂PO₄²⁻

Remove one H⁺: H₂PO₄⁻ − H⁺ = HPO₄²⁻ (one fewer H, charge one more negative). H₃PO₄ is its conjugate acid; PO₄³⁻ differs by two protons.

In the equilibrium CH₃COOH + HSO₄⁻ ⇌ CH₃COOH₂⁺ + SO₄²⁻, which species on the left is acting as the Brønsted–Lowry acid?

  1. CH₃COOH
  2. HSO₄⁻
  3. CH₃COOH₂⁺
  4. SO₄²⁻

HSO₄⁻ loses H⁺ to become SO₄²⁻, so it is the acid; CH₃COOH gains H⁺ and acts as the base here. A species that is normally an acid can act as a base towards a stronger acid.

Predict first: identify the two conjugate pairs in H₂O + CO₃²⁻ ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + OH⁻

Water donates H⁺ to carbonate. Pairs: H₂O / OH⁻ (acid/base) and HCO₃⁻ / CO₃²⁻ (acid/base). This is why sodium carbonate solution is alkaline.

R3.1.3 Amphiprotic species

DefinitionAn amphiprotic species can both donate and accept a proton, so it can act as a Brønsted–Lowry acid or base. An amphoteric species can react as an acid and as a base (by any theory).

Water is the classic amphiprotic species:

as an acid: H₂O(l) + NH₃(aq) ⇌ OH⁻(aq) + NH₄⁺(aq)    as a base: H₂O(l) + HCl(aq) → H₃O⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq)

Other amphiprotic species contain both a removable H and a lone pair: HCO₃⁻, HSO₄⁻, H₂PO₄⁻, HPO₄²⁻, and amino acids.

HCO₃⁻ + H₃O⁺ ⇌ H₂CO₃ + H₂O     HCO₃⁻ + OH⁻ ⇌ CO₃²⁻ + H₂O

All amphiprotic species are amphoteric, but not all amphoteric species are amphiprotic. Zinc oxide and aluminium oxide react with both acids and bases, so they are amphoteric, but they contain no H to donate, so they are not amphiprotic:

ZnO + 2H⁺ → Zn²⁺ + H₂O     ZnO + 2OH⁻ + H₂O → [Zn(OH)₄]²⁻
Common mistakeDo not reverse the statement above. "All amphoteric species are amphiprotic" is false: ZnO and Al₂O₃ have no proton to give.

Which species is amphoteric but not amphiprotic?

  1. H₂O
  2. HCO₃⁻
  3. Al₂O₃
  4. HSO₄⁻

Al₂O₃ reacts with both acids and bases but contains no hydrogen, so it cannot donate a proton. The other three can both donate and accept H⁺.

title: The pH scale and the ionic product of water
html:
R3.1.4 The pH scale

The pH scale (normally 0 to 14 for the solutions you meet) measures how acidic or alkaline a solution is. It can be measured with universal indicator or a pH probe. Everyday substances span the whole range: stomach acid and lemon juice near the bottom, pure water at 7, soap, bleach and oven cleaner near the top.

pH measures the concentration of hydrogen ions on a logarithmic scale ("p" means −log10):

pH = −log10[H⁺]      [H⁺] = 10−pH
  • A change of 1 pH unit = a 10-fold change in [H⁺]. A change of 3 units = 1000-fold.
  • Lower pH = higher [H⁺] = more acidic. pH has no units.
  • pH can be measured with universal indicator (approximate, colour) or a calibrated pH meter/probe (precise, works in coloured solutions, can log data).

On your calculator, "−log" gives pH from [H⁺]; the inverse ("shift log", 10x) gives [H⁺] from pH.

Worked exampleBlack coffee has pH 5 and toothpaste pH 8. Which is more acidic and by what factor?
  1. [H⁺] coffee = 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³; [H⁺] toothpaste = 10⁻⁸ mol dm⁻³.
  2. Ratio = 10⁻⁵ / 10⁻⁸ = 10³. Coffee has 1000 times the [H⁺] of toothpaste.

Solution X has pH 2 and solution Y has pH 5. How do their hydrogen ion concentrations compare?

  1. [H⁺] in X is 3 times that in Y
  2. [H⁺] in X is 1000 times that in Y
  3. [H⁺] in Y is 1000 times that in X
  4. [H⁺] in X is 2.5 times that in Y

A difference of 3 pH units is a factor of 10³. The lower pH (X) has the higher [H⁺]. "3 times" ignores the logarithmic scale.

Strong acids: assume complete dissociation, so [H⁺] = concentration of acid × number of H⁺ released. (For weak acids we cannot make this assumption and Ka is needed – AHL. For bases we first need Kw, below.)

Worked example(a) pH of 0.50 mol dm⁻³ HCl: pH = −log 0.50 = 0.30.
(b) pH of 0.10 mol dm⁻³ H₂SO₄, treating it as releasing 2 H⁺: [H⁺] = 0.20 mol dm⁻³, pH = −log 0.20 = 0.70. (In reality the second dissociation, HSO₄⁻ ⇌ H⁺ + SO₄²⁻, is not complete, so the true pH is slightly higher; follow the question's instructions.)
(c) A solution with pH 2.50: [H⁺] = 10−2.50 = 3.16 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³.
(d) 0.005 g of HCl in 120 cm³: n = 0.005 / 36.46 = 1.37 × 10⁻⁴ mol; c = 1.37 × 10⁻⁴ / 0.120 = 1.14 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³; pH = 2.94.

Calculate the concentration of hydrochloric acid that has a pH of 2.00.

[H⁺] = 10−2.00 = 1.00 × 10⁻² mol dm⁻³. HCl is strong and monoprotic, so [HCl] = 0.0100 mol dm⁻³. (A strong acid solution cannot have pH 12 – that would be alkaline.)

Calculate the pH of 0.025 mol dm⁻³ nitric acid.

HNO₃ is a strong monoprotic acid: [H⁺] = 0.025 mol dm⁻³. pH = −log 0.025 = 1.60.

A solution of a strong acid has pH 3.70. Calculate [H⁺].

[H⁺] = 10−3.70 = 2.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³.
Exam tipDilution by a factor of 10 raises the pH of a strong acid by exactly 1 unit. For a weak acid the pH rises by only about 0.5 per 10-fold dilution, because more of it dissociates as it is diluted.

R3.1.5 The ionic product of water, Kw

Water self-ionizes very slightly (it is amphiprotic, so one molecule can give a proton to another):

H₂O(l) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq)    or    2H₂O(l) ⇌ H₃O⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq)

Writing the equilibrium expression gives Kc = [H⁺][OH⁻] / [H₂O]. The equilibrium lies so far to the left that the numerator is tiny and [H₂O] is huge and effectively constant (about 55.5 mol dm⁻³). Multiplying both sides by [H₂O] absorbs it into a new constant:

Kc × [H₂O] = Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 298 K    (units mol² dm⁻⁶)
  • Neutral: [H⁺] = [OH⁻]. Acidic: [H⁺] > [OH⁻]. Basic: [H⁺] < [OH⁻].
  • At 298 K neutral water has [H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ mol dm⁻³, pH 7.00.
  • In any aqueous solution at 298 K, [H⁺] and [OH⁻] are linked: if you know one, you know the other (rearrange Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻]).
  • Kw depends on temperature (see the AHL section), so "pH 7 = neutral" is only true at 298 K. Kw is in the data booklet.
Worked exampleA solution at 298 K has [H⁺] = 4.60 × 10⁻⁸ mol dm⁻³. Find [OH⁻] and classify it.
  1. [OH⁻] = Kw / [H⁺] = 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ / 4.60 × 10⁻⁸ = 2.17 × 10⁻⁷ mol dm⁻³.
  2. [OH⁻] > [H⁺], so the solution is (very slightly) basic; pH = 7.34.

At 298 K a solution has [OH⁻] = 2.5 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³. Calculate [H⁺].

[H⁺] = Kw/[OH⁻] = 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ / 2.5 × 10⁻³ = 4.0 × 10⁻¹² mol dm⁻³ (pH 11.40, alkaline).

Which statement about pure water at 298 K is correct?

  1. [H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ mol dm⁻³
  2. [H⁺] = [OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ mol dm⁻³
  3. [H⁺] > [OH⁻] because water is a weak acid
  4. It contains no ions at all

Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ and in pure water the two are equal, so each is √(1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴) = 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ mol dm⁻³.

The ionic product links acidity and alkalinity: as one goes up, the other goes down, so their product stays at Kw.

title: Strong and weak acids and bases; neutralization
html:
R3.1.6 Strong and weak acids and bases

DefinitionA strong acid or base is (almost) completely ionized/dissociated in aqueous solution. A weak acid or base is only partially ionized; an equilibrium is set up that lies well to the left.

Strictly, dissociate means to break an ionic compound into its ions and ionize means to form ions (used for covalent molecules such as HCl). For acids and bases the IB uses the two terms interchangeably.

StrongWeak
AcidsHCl, HBr, HI, HNO₃, H₂SO₄ (first proton)Carboxylic acids (CH₃COOH, HCOOH), H₂CO₃ (CO₂(aq)), HF, HCN, H₃PO₄, NH₄⁺
BasesGroup 1 hydroxides (LiOH, NaOH, KOH), Ba(OH)₂NH₃, amines (CH₃NH₂ …), CO₃²⁻, CH₃COO⁻
EquationHCl(aq) → H⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) (single arrow)CH₃COOH(aq) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + CH₃COO⁻(aq) (equilibrium arrow)

A weak base such as ammonia gets its OH⁻ by taking a proton from water: NH₃(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ NH₄⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq). The names and Ka/Kb values of common weak acids and bases are in the data booklet.

Common mistakeStrong ≠ concentrated. Strength is about the extent of ionization; concentration is about how much acid is dissolved per dm³. You can have dilute HCl (strong but dilute) and concentrated ethanoic acid (weak but concentrated). Note also: phosphoric acid H₃PO₄ is a weak acid, despite sometimes being listed with the strong acids.

Picture four beakers: 2 mol dm⁻³ HCl (strong, concentrated), 2 mol dm⁻³ CH₃COOH (weak, concentrated), 0.1 mol dm⁻³ HCl (strong, dilute) and 0.1 mol dm⁻³ CH₃COOH (weak, dilute). In both HCl beakers essentially every molecule has given up its proton; in both ethanoic acid beakers only around 1% has.

Which solution is both weak and concentrated?

  1. 0.01 mol dm⁻³ HNO₃
  2. 5 mol dm⁻³ CH₃COOH
  3. 5 mol dm⁻³ HCl
  4. 0.01 mol dm⁻³ NH₃

Ethanoic acid is weak (partially ionized) and 5 mol dm⁻³ is concentrated. 0.01 mol dm⁻³ NH₃ is weak but dilute; the other two are strong acids.

Distinguishing strong and weak acids of the same concentration (e.g. 1.0 mol dm⁻³ HCl vs 1.0 mol dm⁻³ CH₃COOH):

MethodStrong acidWeak acidReason
pH (meter or UI)Lower pHHigher pHHigher [H⁺]
Electrical conductivity (conductivity meter)HigherLowerMore mobile ions in solution
Rate with Mg or CaCO₃Faster bubblingSlowerRate depends on [H⁺]

As a rough guide for ~0.1–1 mol dm⁻³ solutions: strong acids pH 0–3, weak acids pH 3–6, weak bases pH 8–11, strong bases pH 11–14 – but always remember pH depends on concentration as well as strength.

Equal volumes of equal concentrations of the two acids need the same volume of NaOH to neutralize and produce the same total volume of H₂ with excess Mg: as H⁺ is used up, the weak acid's equilibrium shifts right to replace it. Only the rate differs.

25 cm³ portions of 0.1 mol dm⁻³ HCl and 0.1 mol dm⁻³ CH₃COOH are each titrated with 0.1 mol dm⁻³ NaOH. What is true?

  1. HCl needs a larger volume of NaOH
  2. CH₃COOH needs a larger volume of NaOH
  3. Both need the same volume of NaOH
  4. CH₃COOH cannot be neutralized completely

Both contain 2.5 × 10⁻³ mol of acid that can donate one proton. As NaOH removes H⁺, the weak acid equilibrium shifts right until all of it has reacted.

Key pointA pH meter measures the potential of a glass electrode, not conductivity. Conductivity is a separate measurement (a conductivity meter) that also distinguishes strong from weak because strong electrolytes have more ions.

R3.1.7 Neutralization reactions

In a neutralization an acid reacts with a base to form a salt and (usually) water. The reactions are exothermic. The ionic equation for any strong acid + strong base is:

H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l)

Sodium hydroxide (pH 14) and hydrochloric acid (pH 1) neutralize each other to give sodium chloride solution (pH 7). The Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions are spectator ions; they stay in solution and could be recovered as the salt by evaporating the water.

Common alkalis: NaOH, KOH, Ca(OH)₂, aqueous ammonia. Common insoluble bases contain O²⁻ (metal oxides), OH⁻ (insoluble metal hydroxides) or CO₃²⁻ (metal carbonates). Common acids: H₂SO₄ (sulfuric), HCl (hydrochloric), HNO₃ (nitric), CH₃COOH (ethanoic, in vinegar).

Reaction typeExampleObservation
acid + metal hydroxide → salt + water2NaOH(aq) + H₂SO₄(aq) → Na₂SO₄(aq) + 2H₂O(l)temperature rise
acid + metal oxide → salt + water2HCl(aq) + MgO(s) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l)solid dissolves
acid + carbonate → salt + water + CO₂2HCl(aq) + CaCO₃(s) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g)effervescence; gas turns limewater cloudy
acid + hydrogencarbonate → salt + water + CO₂HCl(aq) + NaHCO₃(s) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g)effervescence
acid + ammonia → ammonium salt2NH₃(aq) + H₂SO₄(aq) → (NH₄)₂SO₄(aq)no gas

Reactive metal + acid → salt + hydrogen (e.g. Mg + H₂SO₄ → MgSO₄ + H₂; 2Na + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂; H₂ gives a squeaky pop with a lighted splint) is a redox reaction, not a proton-transfer neutralization – see R3.2.4.

Naming salts: first part from the base/metal, second part from the acid: HCl → chlorides, HNO₃ → nitrates, H₂SO₄ → sulfates, CH₃COOH → ethanoates, H₃PO₄ → phosphates. Always include state symbols.

Formulae of salts: a salt is made of a positive metal ion (or NH₄⁺) and the negative ion from the acid. Group 1 metals form +1 ions, group 2 form +2; for transition metals the Roman numeral gives the charge, e.g. copper(II) is Cu²⁺. The charges must add up to zero.

BaseAcidSalt
calcium hydroxidehydrochloric acidcalcium chloride, CaCl₂
magnesium oxidenitric acidmagnesium nitrate, Mg(NO₃)₂
calcium carbonatesulfuric acidcalcium sulfate, CaSO₄
aluminium hydroxidenitric acidaluminium nitrate, Al(NO₃)₃
potassium hydroxidesulfuric acidpotassium sulfate, K₂SO₄

When NaOH solution, an alkali, is mixed with hydrochloric acid they neutralize each other, forming a salt and water. Nitric acid makes nitrates and sulfuric acid makes sulfates.

Which equation is correctly balanced?

  1. HCl + Na → NaCl + H₂
  2. 2HCl + MgO → 2MgCl₂ + H₂O
  3. 2HCl + Na₂CO₃ → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂
  4. H₂SO₄ + NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + H₂O

Count atoms on each side: 2 Na, 2 Cl, 2 H, 1 C, 3 O on both sides. The first needs 2HCl + 2Na; the second should give MgCl₂ (not 2MgCl₂); the last needs 2NaOH and 2H₂O.

Which acid and base would you use to make each salt? Write the equation.
  1. Sodium sulfate: 2NaOH(aq) + H₂SO₄(aq) → Na₂SO₄(aq) + 2H₂O(l)
  2. Calcium chloride (with hydrogen): Ca(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂(g) (redox)
  3. Copper(II) nitrate: CuO(s) + 2HNO₃(aq) → Cu(NO₃)₂(aq) + H₂O(l)
  4. Iron(II) sulfate (with CO₂): FeCO₃(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → FeSO₄(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g)
  5. Lithium sulfate: 2LiOH(aq) + H₂SO₄(aq) → Li₂SO₄(aq) + 2H₂O(l)
  6. Magnesium nitrate from an oxide: MgO(s) + 2HNO₃(aq) → Mg(NO₃)₂(aq) + H₂O(l)
  7. Magnesium nitrate from a hydroxide: Mg(OH)₂(s) + 2HNO₃(aq) → Mg(NO₃)₂(aq) + 2H₂O(l)
Key point"Neutralization" means the acid and base have reacted in stoichiometric amounts – the resulting salt solution is only pH 7 if both parents are strong. Salts of weak acids or weak bases give solutions that are not neutral (AHL, R3.1.12).

Acid deposition (context)

Rain is naturally slightly acidic (pH ≈ 5.6) because CO₂ dissolves: H₂O(l) + CO₂(g) ⇌ H₂CO₃(aq). Acid deposition has pH below 5.6 and forms when sulfur and nitrogen oxides (primary pollutants from burning fossil fuels and from vehicle engines) dissolve to give H₂SO₃, H₂SO₄, HNO₂ and HNO₃. Because acid deposition can fall far from its source, often in another country, solving it needs international cooperation.

S + O₂ → SO₂    SO₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₃    2SO₂ + O₂ → 2SO₃    SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄
N₂ + O₂ → 2NO    2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂    2NO₂ + H₂O → HNO₂ + HNO₃

title: Titrations and pH curves (practical skills)
html:
R3.1.8 pH curves and titration (strong acid + strong base)

In an acid–base titration a solution of known concentration (the titrant) is added from a burette to a measured volume (pipette) of the other solution (the analyte) until the equivalence point is reached. Following the pH with a pH meter gives a pH curve.

DefinitionThe equivalence point is where stoichiometrically equivalent amounts of acid and base have reacted. The end point is where the indicator changes colour; a good indicator makes the end point coincide with the equivalence point.
Do now: how could you tell the end point had been reached without an indicator?

Use a pH meter (look for the sudden large change in pH), a conductivity meter (conductivity reaches a minimum for strong acid + strong base), or a thermometer (the temperature stops rising once neutralization is complete – a thermometric titration).

Strong acid (e.g. 25.0 cm³ 0.100 mol dm⁻³ HCl) titrated with strong base (0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH):

  • Starts at a low pH (≈1), rises only slowly at first.
  • Very steep, near-vertical jump from about pH 3 to pH 11 at the equivalence point (25.0 cm³).
  • pH at equivalence = 7 (NaCl does not hydrolyse).
  • Levels off at a high pH (≈12–13) as excess NaOH is added.

If the acid is added to the base instead, the curve is the mirror image: it starts high and falls. Always check which solution is in the flask.

Because the vertical section is so long, almost any common indicator (methyl orange, bromothymol blue, phenolphthalein) works for strong acid + strong base.

Exam tipRead the equivalence volume from the middle of the vertical section, then use n = cV and the mole ratio to find the unknown concentration (see R2.1). A pH meter has advantages over an indicator: no subjective colour judgment, works with coloured solutions, and gives the whole curve (and so pKa for a weak acid).

25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ HCl is titrated with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH. What is the approximate pH after 35 cm³ of NaOH?

  1. 1
  2. 7
  3. 9
  4. 12

After equivalence (25 cm³) the extra 10 cm³ of NaOH is in excess: [OH⁻] = (0.0010 mol)/(0.060 dm³) = 0.017 mol dm⁻³, pOH 1.8, pH ≈ 12.2. The plateau is set by the excess titrant.

Practical: titration with a pH meter

  1. Rinse the electrode with distilled water and calibrate the meter with standard buffer solutions (pH 4 and/or pH 10, depending on the range you expect).
  2. Pipette 25.0 cm³ of the solution in the flask (about 0.1 mol dm⁻³) into a 250 cm³ beaker, add a stir bar and stir steadily on a magnetic stirrer without hitting the electrode.
  3. Immerse the electrode (add distilled water if needed so the bulb is covered – this does not change the amount of acid or base).
  4. Record the initial pH, then add the titrant from the burette in 1 cm³ portions, recording the pH each time.
  5. Within about 5 cm³ of the expected equivalence point, reduce the additions to 0.5 cm³ and then 0.1 cm³ so the steep section is well defined.
  6. Continue for about 5 cm³ past the equivalence point, then repeat with the second acid and plot both curves on the same axes.

Safety: the glass electrode is fragile and must not be allowed to dry out. The neutralized salt solutions can normally be disposed of down the sink.

Questions from the practical: which acid was weak, and what advantage does the pH meter give?
  • The weak acid curve starts at a higher pH, has a buffer region and a shorter vertical section with equivalence pH above 7.
  • The meter gives a continuous record, is not affected by colour, avoids judging a colour change, and lets you read pKa at half-equivalence (HL).
  • An acidic buffer is a weak acid with its conjugate base, e.g. CH₃COOH with CH₃COONa (HL).

Titration calculations

25.0 cm³ of a saturated strontium hydroxide solution needs 32.8 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ HCl for neutralization. Sr(OH)₂ + 2HCl → SrCl₂ + 2H₂O. Calculate the concentration of Sr(OH)₂ in mol dm⁻³.

n(HCl) = 0.0328 × 0.100 = 3.28 × 10⁻³ mol. n(Sr(OH)₂) = ½ × 3.28 × 10⁻³ = 1.64 × 10⁻³ mol. c = 1.64 × 10⁻³ / 0.0250 = 0.0656 mol dm⁻³ (= 0.0656 × 121.64 = 7.98 g dm⁻³).

Practical: the percentage of nitrogen in a fertiliser (back titration)

Ammonium salts in fertilisers cannot be titrated directly with a simple acid–base titration, so a back titration is used. The fertiliser (here ammonium sulfate) is boiled with a known excess of NaOH, which drives off all the nitrogen as ammonia; the NaOH left over is then titrated with standard HCl.

NH₄⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → NH₃(g) + H₂O(l)
  1. Weigh about 1.7 g of fertiliser accurately into a conical flask; pipette in 25.0 cm³ of ~2 mol dm⁻³ NaOH (excess).
  2. Boil gently (fume cupboard: ammonia is released) until moist red litmus held in the steam no longer turns blue – all the NH₃ has gone. Top up with distilled water so it does not boil dry.
  3. Titrate the remaining NaOH with 1.00 mol dm⁻³ HCl using bromothymol blue (blue → green).
  4. Standardise the NaOH separately: titrate 10.0 cm³ portions with the same HCl.
Worked exampleStandardisation: 10.0 cm³ NaOH needed a mean titre of 19.67 cm³ of 1.00 mol dm⁻³ HCl (concordant titres 19.70, 19.60, 19.70; the rough titre is left out), so c(NaOH) = 1.00 × 19.67/10.0 = 1.967 mol dm⁻³.
  1. n(NaOH) added to sample A = 1.967 × 0.0250 = 0.0492 mol.
  2. Back titration of sample A needed 17.50 cm³ HCl: n(NaOH left) = 1.00 × 0.01750 = 0.0175 mol.
  3. n(NaOH that reacted with NH₄⁺) = 0.0492 − 0.0175 = 0.0317 mol = n(N).
  4. Mass of N = 0.0317 × 14.01 = 0.444 g. Mass of fertiliser = 3.242 − 1.182 = 2.060 g.
  5. % N = 0.444 / 2.060 × 100 = 21.6%. (Samples B and C give 21.5% and 21.8%; mean 21.6%.)
The theoretical value for pure (NH₄)₂SO₄ is 2 × 14.01 / 132.17 × 100 = 21.2%.

Sample B: 1.945 g of fertiliser; the excess NaOH (0.0492 mol added) needed 19.40 cm³ of 1.00 mol dm⁻³ HCl. Calculate the percentage of nitrogen.

n(NaOH left) = 0.01940 mol; n(N) = 0.0492 − 0.0194 = 0.0298 mol; m(N) = 0.0298 × 14.01 = 0.417 g; % N = 0.417/1.945 × 100 = 21.5%.

Uncertainties. Percentage uncertainty = absolute uncertainty / measured value × 100%. When quantities are multiplied or divided, add their percentage uncertainties. Typical values: 50 cm³ burette ±0.05 cm³ per reading, 25 cm³ pipette ±0.06 cm³, 10 cm³ pipette ±0.04 cm³, 3 d.p. balance ±0.0005 g per reading. Percentage error = |accepted − experimental| / accepted × 100%.

Evaluation: the mean was 21.6% against an accepted 21.2%. What does this tell you?
  • The result is about 2% above the accepted value, larger than the spread of the replicates (±0.1%) but within the combined instrumental uncertainty (about ±0.7%).
  • The replicates agree very closely, so random errors were small (or the same apparatus repeated the same error each time).
  • Not boiling for long enough would leave NH₃ behind and give a low result, so that systematic error was not significant here. A real fertiliser may also contain other nitrogen compounds.
  • Improvements: standardise the HCl accurately against a primary standard such as anhydrous sodium carbonate, and use grade A rather than grade B glassware.

In the back titration, why is the NaOH added in excess?

  1. So that the indicator works
  2. So that all of the ammonium ions react and all the NH₃ is driven off
  3. To neutralize the sulfate ions
  4. To make the solution a buffer

Only with excess OH⁻ is every NH₄⁺ converted to NH₃; the amount of NaOH that reacted is then found by titrating what is left.

title: pOH, Kw and temperature, Ka and Kb (AHL)
html:
R3.1.9 pOH and the temperature dependence of Kw AHL

pOH = −log[OH⁻]    [OH⁻] = 10−pOH    pKw = pH + pOH = 14.00 at 298 K

For strong bases, assume complete dissociation, then use Kw (or pOH). The main thing to remember: you cannot take −log of [OH⁻] and call it pH.

Worked examplepH of 0.40 mol dm⁻³ NaOH at 298 K.
  1. Strong base, fully dissociated: [OH⁻] = 0.40 mol dm⁻³.
  2. Route 1: [H⁺] = Kw/[OH⁻] = 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ / 0.40 = 2.5 × 10⁻¹⁴; pH = −log(2.5 × 10⁻¹⁴) = 13.60.
  3. Route 2: pOH = −log 0.40 = 0.40; pH = 14.00 − 0.40 = 13.60.
For Ba(OH)₂, remember [OH⁻] = 2 × concentration.

Calculate the pH of 0.10 mol dm⁻³ Ba(OH)₂ at 298 K.

[OH⁻] = 2 × 0.10 = 0.20 mol dm⁻³; pOH = −log 0.20 = 0.70; pH = 14.00 − 0.70 = 13.30.

Calculate the pH of the solution formed when 100 cm³ of water is added to 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH.

n(OH⁻) = 0.0250 × 0.100 = 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol in 0.125 dm³: [OH⁻] = 0.0200 mol dm⁻³. pOH = 1.70, pH = 12.30.

20.0 cm³ of 0.500 mol dm⁻³ NaOH is mixed with 80.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol dm⁻³ HNO₃. Calculate the pH.

n(OH⁻) = 0.0100 mol; n(H⁺) = 0.0160 mol. Excess H⁺ = 0.0060 mol in 0.100 dm³ = 0.060 mol dm⁻³. pH = −log 0.060 = 1.22.

The self-ionization of water is endothermic (bonds are broken). Raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium right (Le Châtelier), so Kw increases and the pH of pure water falls below 7 – but the water is still neutral because [H⁺] still equals [OH⁻].

Worked exampleAt 373 K, Kw = 51.3 × 10⁻¹⁴. Find the pH of pure water.
  1. [H⁺] = [OH⁻], so [H⁺]² = Kw; [H⁺] = √(51.3 × 10⁻¹⁴) = 7.16 × 10⁻⁷ mol dm⁻³.
  2. pH = −log(7.16 × 10⁻⁷) = 6.14. The water is neutral (not acidic) at this temperature.

Pure water at 323 K has pH 6.63. Which statement is correct?

  1. The water is acidic
  2. The water is neutral, and Kw is larger than at 298 K
  3. Kw is smaller than at 298 K
  4. The ionization of water is exothermic

In pure water [H⁺] = [OH⁻] at any temperature, so it is neutral. A lower pH means larger [H⁺] and so larger Kw, consistent with an endothermic ionization.

R3.1.10 Ka, Kb, pKa and pKb AHL

For weak acids we cannot assume [H⁺] = [HA], because weak acids do not dissociate fully, so we use the equilibrium constant for the ionization (the acid dissociation constant):

HA(aq) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + A⁻(aq)    Ka = [H⁺][A⁻] / [HA]
B(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ BH⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq)    Kb = [BH⁺][OH⁻] / [B]
pKa = −log Ka    Ka = 10−pKa    pKb = −log Kb
  • Larger Ka (smaller pKa) = stronger acid. Larger Kb (smaller pKb) = stronger base. pKa is to Ka what pH is to [H⁺].
  • Values for common weak acids and bases are in the data booklet. Like all K values they depend only on temperature.

Assumptions for a weak acid calculation: (1) [H⁺] = [A⁻] (water's own H⁺ is negligible); (2) the acid is so slightly ionized that [HA]eqm ≈ [HA]initial. Then (except in buffers, where [A⁻] ≠ [H⁺]):

Ka ≈ [H⁺]² / [HA]initial   ⇒   [H⁺] = √(Ka × [HA])
Worked exampleCalculate the pH of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid (pKa = 4.76).
  1. Ka = 10−4.76 = 1.74 × 10⁻⁵.
  2. [H⁺]² = 1.74 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.100 = 1.74 × 10⁻⁶; [H⁺] = 1.32 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³.
  3. pH = −log(1.32 × 10⁻³) = 2.88. (Check: only 1.3% ionized, so assumption 2 is fine.)
Worked exampleCalculate the pH of 0.010 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid, Ka = 1.15 × 10⁻⁵ at the temperature used.
  1. [H⁺]² = 1.15 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.010 = 1.15 × 10⁻⁷.
  2. [H⁺] = 3.39 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³; pH = 3.47.
Worked exampleA weak acid HA has pKa = 3.42. Find the pH of a 0.040 mol dm⁻³ solution.
  1. Ka = 10−3.42 = 3.80 × 10⁻⁴.
  2. [H⁺]² = 3.80 × 10⁻⁴ × 0.040 = 1.52 × 10⁻⁵; [H⁺] = 3.90 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³.
  3. pH = 2.41.
Worked exampleFinding Ka from pH: 0.050 mol dm⁻³ HA has pH 3.00.
  1. [H⁺] = [A⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³.
  2. Ka = (1.0 × 10⁻³)² / 0.050 = 2.0 × 10⁻⁵; pKa = 4.70.
Worked exampleWeak base: pH of 0.10 mol dm⁻³ NH₃ (pKb = 4.75).
  1. Kb = 10−4.75 = 1.78 × 10⁻⁵.
  2. [OH⁻] = √(1.78 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.10) = 1.33 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³; pOH = 2.88.
  3. pH = 14.00 − 2.88 = 11.12.

Calculate pKa when Ka = 1.24 × 10⁻⁵.

pKa = −log(1.24 × 10⁻⁵) = 4.91.

Calculate the pH of 0.150 mol dm⁻³ benzoic acid (benzenecarboxylic acid), pKa = 4.20.

Ka = 10−4.20 = 6.31 × 10⁻⁵. [H⁺] = √(6.31 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.150) = 3.08 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³. pH = 2.51.

Calculate the pH of 1.00 mol dm⁻³ methanoic acid, Ka = 1.78 × 10⁻⁴.

[H⁺] = √(1.78 × 10⁻⁴ × 1.00) = 1.33 × 10⁻² mol dm⁻³; pH = 1.87.

A 0.100 mol dm⁻³ solution of phenylethanoic acid has pH 2.66. Calculate Ka.

[H⁺] = 10−2.66 = 2.19 × 10⁻³. Ka = (2.19 × 10⁻³)²/0.100 = 4.79 × 10⁻⁵.

What concentration of ethanoic acid (Ka = 1.74 × 10⁻⁵) has pH 4.53?

[H⁺] = 10−4.53 = 2.95 × 10⁻⁵. [HA] = [H⁺]²/Ka = 8.71 × 10⁻¹⁰ / 1.74 × 10⁻⁵ = 5.00 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³. (At this low concentration the approximations are poor – a good point to discuss.)

Which acid is stronger: ethanoic acid (pKa 4.76) or propanoic acid (pKa 4.87)?

  1. Ethanoic acid
  2. Propanoic acid
  3. They are equally strong
  4. Cannot tell without concentrations

Smaller pKa = larger Ka = stronger acid. Strength is a property of the acid, independent of concentration.

R3.1.11 Ka × Kb = Kw for a conjugate pair AHL

Multiplying Ka for HA by Kb for its conjugate base A⁻ cancels everything except [H⁺][OH⁻]:

Ka × Kb = Kw     pKa + pKb = pKw = 14.00 (at 298 K)

This shows quantitatively that the stronger the acid, the weaker its conjugate base.

Worked examplepKa(CH₃COOH) = 4.76. Find pKb and Kb of CH₃COO⁻.
  1. pKb = 14.00 − 4.76 = 9.24.
  2. Kb = 10−9.24 = 5.75 × 10⁻¹⁰.
Similarly, pKa(NH₄⁺) = 14.00 − 4.75 = 9.25.

The pKb of methylamine is 3.34. Calculate pKa of the methylammonium ion, CH₃NH₃⁺, at 298 K.

pKa = 14.00 − 3.34 = 10.66.

title: Salt hydrolysis, pH curves and indicators (AHL)
html:
R3.1.12 The pH of salt solutions (salt hydrolysis) AHL

A salt's solution is not always neutral. Salt hydrolysis is the reaction of a cation or an anion with water. Ions derived from a weak parent acid or base react with water, releasing OH⁻ or H⁺:

anion hydrolysis (pH > 7): A⁻(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ HA(aq) + OH⁻(aq)     cation hydrolysis (pH < 7): BH⁺(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ B(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq)
Parent acid + baseExample saltIon that hydrolysespH at 298 K
strong + strongNaCl, KNO₃neither≈ 7
weak acid + strong baseCH₃COONa, Na₂CO₃anion: CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COOH + OH⁻> 7
strong acid + weak baseNH₄Clcation: NH₄⁺ + H₂O ⇌ NH₃ + H₃O⁺< 7
weak acid + weak baseCH₃COONH₄bothdepends on relative Ka and Kb

Highly charged small metal ions (high charge density, e.g. Al³⁺, Fe³⁺) also give acidic solutions. Charge density is the ratio of an ion's charge to its size (volume), so it rises with charge and falls with ionic radius. The small, highly charged ion polarizes and weakens the O–H bonds of the water ligands, which release H⁺:

[Al(H₂O)₆]³⁺(aq) ⇌ [Al(H₂O)₅(OH)]²⁺(aq) + H⁺(aq)     [Fe(H₂O)₆]³⁺(aq) ⇌ [Fe(H₂O)₅(OH)]²⁺(aq) + H⁺(aq)
Worked examplepH of 0.10 mol dm⁻³ sodium ethanoate (Kb(CH₃COO⁻) = 5.75 × 10⁻¹⁰).
  1. [OH⁻] = √(5.75 × 10⁻¹⁰ × 0.10) = 7.58 × 10⁻⁶ mol dm⁻³.
  2. pOH = 5.12; pH = 8.88 – basic, as predicted.

Which 0.1 mol dm⁻³ solution has the lowest pH?

  1. NaCl
  2. CH₃COONa
  3. AlCl₃
  4. Na₂CO₃

The hexaaquaaluminium ion is acidic because of the high charge density of Al³⁺. NaCl is neutral; ethanoate and carbonate are basic (anion hydrolysis).

Calculate the pH of 0.20 mol dm⁻³ NH₄Cl at 298 K (pKa of NH₄⁺ = 9.25).

NH₄⁺ is a weak acid: Ka = 10−9.25 = 5.62 × 10⁻¹⁰. [H⁺] = √(5.62 × 10⁻¹⁰ × 0.20) = √(1.12 × 10⁻¹⁰) = 1.06 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³. pH = 4.97 – acidic, as predicted for a salt of a strong acid and a weak base.

R3.1.13 pH curves for weak acids and bases AHL

TitrationStart pHVertical sectionpH at equivalenceSuitable indicator
strong acid + strong base≈ 1long, ≈ pH 3–117almost any
weak acid + strong base≈ 3shorter, ≈ pH 7–11> 7 (≈ 8–9)phenolphthalein
strong acid + weak base≈ 1≈ pH 3–7< 7 (≈ 5)methyl orange / methyl red
weak acid + weak base≈ 3no sharp jump≈ 7 (depends)none suitable – use a pH meter

The pH at the equivalence point depends on whether the salt formed is acidic, neutral or basic – which is exactly the salt hydrolysis above.

Key features of the weak acid + strong base curve (e.g. CH₃COOH + NaOH):

  • Higher starting pH than a strong acid of the same concentration (partial ionization).
  • A small initial rise, then a gently sloping buffer region: the solution contains both HA and A⁻, so small additions of base change the pH very little.
  • Half-equivalence point: half the acid has been converted to A⁻, so [HA] = [A⁻] and Ka = [H⁺], i.e. pH = pKa. This is how pKa is found experimentally.
  • Equivalence pH > 7 because the salt's anion (CH₃COO⁻) hydrolyses.

For a weak base titrated with a strong acid, at half-equivalence pOH = pKb (and pH = pKa of the conjugate acid BH⁺). The curve starts high (weak base), falls gently through a buffer region, drops steeply and has its equivalence point below 7.

Worked exampleA weak acid is titrated with NaOH. Equivalence is at 22.0 cm³ (pH 9.5). At 11.0 cm³ the pH is 5.4. State pKa and Ka.
  1. 11.0 cm³ is the half-equivalence volume, so pKa = pH = 5.4.
  2. Ka = 10−5.4 = 4.0 × 10⁻⁶.
Exam tipWhen sketching curves, label: initial pH, equivalence volume and pH, the buffer region, the half-equivalence point, and the final pH plateau. The final plateau is set by the excess titrant, not by the analyte.

In a titration of 20.0 cm³ of 0.10 mol dm⁻³ NH₃ with 0.10 mol dm⁻³ HCl, at what volume of HCl does pH = pKa(NH₄⁺)?

  1. 0 cm³
  2. 10.0 cm³
  3. 20.0 cm³
  4. 40.0 cm³

Equivalence is at 20.0 cm³; at half that (10.0 cm³), [NH₃] = [NH₄⁺], so pOH = pKb and pH = pKa of NH₄⁺.

R3.1.14 Acid–base indicators AHL

An indicator is a weak acid (HIn) (or weak base) whose undissociated form and conjugate base (In⁻) have different colours:

  • High [H⁺] (acid): equilibrium shifts left → colour of HIn.
  • Low [H⁺] (alkali): H⁺ is removed, equilibrium shifts right → colour of In⁻.
  • At the midpoint of the colour change [HIn] = [In⁻], so Ka(HIn) = [H⁺] and pH = pKa(HIn). The visible change happens over roughly pKa ± 1.

All acid–base indicators work in the same way – only their pKa values (and colours) differ. Litmus, for example, is red in acid and blue in alkali.

R3.1.15 Choosing an indicator AHL

Choose an indicator whose colour-change range (pKa ± 1) lies within the vertical (steep) section of the pH curve, ideally including the equivalence-point pH.

IndicatorpH rangeColour change (acid → alkali)Use for
Methyl orange3.1–4.4red → yellowstrong acid + weak base
Methyl red4.4–6.2red → yellowstrong acid + weak base
Bromothymol blue6.0–7.6yellow → bluestrong acid + strong base
Phenolphthalein8.3–10.0colourless → pinkweak acid + strong base

Litmus is not used for titrations because its colour change is gradual and spread over a wide range. Check the data booklet for exact ranges and more indicators.

Which indicator is most suitable for titrating ethanoic acid with sodium hydroxide?

  1. Methyl orange (3.1–4.4)
  2. Methyl red (4.4–6.2)
  3. Phenolphthalein (8.3–10.0)
  4. Any of these

The equivalence point is about pH 8–9 and the vertical section runs roughly from 7 to 11. Methyl orange would change colour in the buffer region, long before equivalence.

Neutral red changes colour between pH 6.8 and 8.0. For which titration would it be suitable?

  1. Strong acid + strong base
  2. Weak acid + weak base
  3. Strong acid + weak base only
  4. None

Its range must lie within the vertical section. Only strong acid + strong base has a vertical section (≈ 3–11) that covers 6.8–8.0.

Sketch the curve, then name an indicator: 25 cm³ of 0.10 mol dm⁻³ HNO₃ in the flask, 0.20 mol dm⁻³ NaOH from the burette.

Strong acid + strong base. Starts at pH 1.0, equivalence at 12.5 cm³ (half the volume because the base is twice as concentrated), pH 7 at equivalence, long vertical section, finishes near pH 13. Bromothymol blue (or phenolphthalein, or methyl orange) is suitable.

title: Buffer solutions (AHL)
html:
R3.1.16 Buffer solutions AHL

Do now: why might we need to keep a pH constant? Where does this matter in real life?

Enzymes and proteins only work in a narrow pH range, so blood must stay at pH ≈ 7.4. pH control also matters in shampoos and cosmetics, food and drink, fermentation, swimming pools, dyeing, and for calibrating pH meters.

DefinitionA buffer solution resists a change in pH when small amounts of acid or base (or water) are added.

A buffer contains significant amounts of a weak acid and its conjugate base (or a weak base and its conjugate acid), so it can "mop up" both added H⁺ and added OH⁻.

Acidic bufferBasic buffer
Made fromweak acid + its salt with a strong base, e.g. CH₃COOH + CH₃COONaweak base + its salt with a strong acid, e.g. NH₃ + NH₄Cl
Add H⁺CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺ → CH₃COOHNH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺
Add OH⁻CH₃COOH + OH⁻ → CH₃COO⁻ + H₂ONH₄⁺ + OH⁻ → NH₃ + H₂O

In the acidic buffer, the salt is fully dissociated (NaCH₃COO → Na⁺ + CH₃COO⁻), providing a large reservoir of CH₃COO⁻, while the weak acid is barely dissociated (CH₃COOH ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺), providing a large reservoir of CH₃COOH. In the basic buffer, NH₄Cl provides the NH₄⁺ and the weak base provides NH₃.

A buffer can also be made by partly neutralizing a weak acid with a strong base (e.g. 2 mol CH₃COOH + 1 mol NaOH gives 1 mol each of CH₃COOH and CH₃COO⁻) – this is exactly what exists in the buffer region of a weak acid/strong base titration.

Exam tipTo explain buffer action for full marks: name the two components, write the equation for reaction with added H⁺ and with added OH⁻, and state that because [HA] and [A⁻] are both large, their ratio (and so the pH) changes very little. A mixture of a strong acid and its salt (HCl + NaCl) is not a buffer.

Which mixture forms a buffer solution?

  1. HCl and NaCl
  2. NaOH and NaCl
  3. 0.20 mol CH₃COOH and 0.10 mol NaOH
  4. 0.10 mol CH₃COOH and 0.20 mol NaOH

Partial neutralization leaves 0.10 mol CH₃COOH and 0.10 mol CH₃COO⁻: a weak acid and its conjugate base. With excess NaOH (last option) no weak acid is left.

A little HCl is added to an NH₃/NH₄Cl buffer. Which reaction removes most of the added H⁺?

  1. NH₄⁺ + H⁺ → NH₅²⁺
  2. NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺
  3. Cl⁻ + H⁺ → HCl
  4. OH⁻ + H⁺ → H₂O only

The base component of the buffer, NH₃, takes up the added protons. Cl⁻ is the conjugate base of a strong acid and does not react.

R3.1.17 The pH of a buffer AHL

Rearranging Ka = [H⁺][A⁻]/[HA] gives [H⁺] = Ka[HA]/[A⁻]; taking −log gives:

pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA])     (and for a basic buffer pOH = pKb + log([BH⁺]/[B]))
  • The pH depends on pKa and on the ratio [A⁻]/[HA]. When [A⁻] = [HA], pH = pKa.
  • Dilution changes both concentrations by the same factor, so the ratio – and pH – stays (almost) the same.
  • A buffer works best within about pKa ± 1; choose a weak acid with pKa close to the pH you want. Buffer capacity is greater when the concentrations are higher.
Worked exampleA buffer contains 0.20 mol dm⁻³ CH₃COOH and 0.10 mol dm⁻³ CH₃COONa (pKa = 4.76). Find its pH.
  1. pH = 4.76 + log(0.10/0.20) = 4.76 − 0.30 = 4.46.
Worked example50.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol dm⁻³ CH₃COOH is mixed with 25.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol dm⁻³ NaOH. Find the pH.
  1. n(CH₃COOH) = 0.0100 mol; n(OH⁻) = 0.00500 mol.
  2. After reaction: CH₃COOH 0.00500 mol, CH₃COO⁻ 0.00500 mol (same total volume, so the ratio of moles = ratio of concentrations).
  3. pH = 4.76 + log(1) = 4.76 – this is the half-equivalence point.
Worked example2.05 g of sodium ethanoate is added to 0.500 dm³ of 0.0100 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid (Ka = 1.74 × 10⁻⁵). Find the pH.
  1. n(CH₃COONa) = 2.05 / 82.04 = 0.0250 mol; [A⁻] = 0.0250 / 0.500 = 0.0500 mol dm⁻³.
  2. [H⁺] = Ka[HA]/[A⁻] = 1.74 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.0100 / 0.0500 = 3.48 × 10⁻⁶ mol dm⁻³.
  3. pH = 5.46.
Worked example25.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid is mixed with 25.0 cm³ of 0.400 mol dm⁻³ NaOH (Ka = 1.74 × 10⁻⁵). (a) Find the pH. (b) Find the new pH after adding 0.20 cm³ of 0.50 mol dm⁻³ H₂SO₄.
  1. (a) n(HA) = 0.0250 × 1.00 = 0.0250 mol; n(OH⁻) = 0.0250 × 0.400 = 0.0100 mol, so HA is in excess. HA + OH⁻ → A⁻ + H₂O leaves HA 0.0150 mol and forms A⁻ 0.0100 mol (both in the same 50.0 cm³, so the volume cancels).
  2. [H⁺] = 1.74 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.0150/0.0100 = 2.61 × 10⁻⁵; pH = 4.58.
  3. (b) n(H⁺) added = 2 × 0.00020 × 0.50 = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol. A⁻ + H⁺ → HA: A⁻ 0.0098 mol, HA 0.0152 mol.
  4. [H⁺] = 1.74 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.0152/0.0098 = 2.70 × 10⁻⁵; pH = 4.57 – a change of only 0.01.

Calculate the pH of a buffer made from 0.150 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid and 0.100 mol dm⁻³ sodium ethanoate (pKa = 4.76).

pH = 4.76 + log(0.100/0.150) = 4.76 − 0.18 = 4.58.

100 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid (pKa 4.76) is mixed with 50.0 cm³ of 0.150 mol dm⁻³ NaOH. Calculate the pH.

n(HA) = 0.0100 mol; n(OH⁻) = 0.00750 mol. After reaction: HA 0.00250 mol, A⁻ 0.00750 mol. pH = 4.76 + log(3.00) = 4.76 + 0.48 = 5.24.

50.0 cm³ of 0.500 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid (pKa 4.76) is added to 50.0 cm³ of 0.250 mol dm⁻³ KOH. Calculate the pH.

n(HA) = 0.0250 mol, n(OH⁻) = 0.0125 mol: exactly half-neutralized, so [HA] = [A⁻] and pH = pKa = 4.76.

20.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ methanoic acid (Ka = 1.7 × 10⁻⁴) is added to 40.0 cm³ of 0.080 mol dm⁻³ KOH. Calculate the pH.

n(HA) = 0.00200 mol; n(OH⁻) = 0.00320 mol. The base is in excess (this is not a buffer): excess OH⁻ = 0.00120 mol in 0.0600 dm³ = 0.0200 mol dm⁻³. pOH 1.70, pH 12.30.
Why does adding 2.00 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH to 100 cm³ of water change the pH by about 4 units, but to 100 cm³ of a buffer only by about 0.02?

In water, the OH⁻ stays in solution: [OH⁻] ≈ 1.96 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³, pH ≈ 11.3 (from 7). In the buffer, the OH⁻ reacts with the weak acid (HA + OH⁻ → A⁻ + H₂O). The ratio [A⁻]/[HA] changes only slightly because both are present in much larger amounts than the added OH⁻, so the pH barely moves.

Real-life buffers: blood is kept at pH ≈ 7.4 mainly by the H₂CO₃/HCO₃⁻ system; buffers are also used in shampoos, food, fermentation and calibrating pH meters (pH 4 and pH 10 buffers).

The pH of a buffer depends on the pKa of the weak acid and the ratio of [A⁻] to [HA].
